catalog_quote: By the same token, processes of vowel reduction which have the effect of altering syllable patterns do not have to be conditioned by stress. For example, in Nkore-Kiga, a language which does not have word stress, high vowels may be deleted in certain consonantal contexts word-medially (Taylor 1985: 202–205).

new_statements.quote: Runyankore is both a tonal language and a syllable-timed language, meaning that every syllable tends to be produced with roughly equal duration and tone (Poletto, 1998). In contrast, English is stress-timed, with rhythm determined by the timing of stressed syllables and a greater use of intonation for pragmatic and emotional meaning. [...] Participants in this study fail to acquire the prosodic rules needed for native-like English fluency because Runyankore does not rely on stress-based rhythm or intonation contours in the same way English does.
new_statements.citation: Nuwahereza, Allan. 2025. Mother tongue interference in the speaking of English among L1 Runyankore-speaking students of Makerere University. Unpublished MA dissertation, Makerere University, Kampala (MakIR hdl 10570/15414).
new_statements.locator: Section 5.2.4 'Tonal and syllable-timed prosody', printed pp. 64-65 (pp. 74-75)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote: (107 pp.), extracted text pp. 74-75 = printed pp. 64-65, section "5.2.4 Tonal and syllable-timed prosody". Both quoted sentences are present word for word: "Runyankore is both a tonal language and a syllable-timed language, meaning that every syllable tends to be produced with roughly equal duration and tone (Poletto, 1998). In contrast, English is stress-timed, with rhythm determined by the timing of stressed syllables and a greater use of intonation for pragmatic and emotional meaning." and, four paragraphs later, "Participants in this study fail to acquire the prosodic rules needed for native-like English fluency because Runyankore does not rely on stress-based rhythm or intonatio…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Runyankore is described as a tone language (H, L, falling per Ndoleriire 2024 as cited) that is syllable-timed and has no stress-based rhythm; nothing is said about a fixed word-stress position. The only first-hand prosodic facts in the opened primary sources (Poletto 1998 WPL; Hyman 2022 SPiL Plus) are tonal: falling tones are confined to a long phrase-penultimate syllable and final H retracts to the penult phrase-finally.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about utterance rhythm (syllable-timing) in L2-English interference, not word-level citation forms; second-hand, attributed to Poletto 1998 whose dissertation could not be opened. Treat as weak.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern Runyankore (Nkore) proper or the joint standard Runyankore-Rukiga; Nkore-Kiga (Taylor 1985) covers Nkore and Kiga (chig1238) together. The Makerere theses treat 'Runyankore' as spoken in Ankole (Mbarara etc.), i.e. nyan1307.

tone_statements.citation: Kaji, Shigeki. 2010. A comparative study of tone of West Ugandan Bantu languages, with particular focus on the tone loss in Tooro. ZAS Papers in Linguistics 53: 99-107. doi:10.21248/zaspil.53.2010.394
tone_statements.quote: The Ankole system basically remains the same as the Haya system, but has moved one step or two toward tone simplification. The characteristics of Ankole tone include the following. 1. As far as the system is concerned the Ankole tone system is the same as the Haya system. 2. There are words which have no high tone (…ss). 3. If a word has high tone, it appears only in one syllable underlyingly (…sśssss, …sśsss, …sśss, …sśs, …sś). 4. Underlying distinctions are generally kept in isolation except in one pattern. That is, although when a word’s penultimate syllable is long and H-toned, this H is realized as F (falling) like Haya, when a word’s penultimate syllable is H-toned but short, this underlying H is realized as H, and not F like Haya, thus confusing the …HL pattern with the …LH patterns in isolation. Both become …HL.
tone_statements.locator: §1 Introduction p.99; §3 'Ankole' pp.101-102 (points 1-6 and examples 3.1-3.6); §6 comparison tables pp.104-105; §8 summary p.106-107

tone_statements.quote: The most characteristic feature of Ankole, Kiga, Tooro, Nyoro, and Haya is that the southern-most language Haya has the most conservative tone system among the five, and the tone system becomes simpler as we go northwards, to the point that Tooro has lost its lexical tone (Nyoro, which is spoken to the north of Tooro, seems to keep its lexical tone). In Tooro, all nouns and verbs are pronounced with a high tone on the penultimate syllable of the word. This must have been brought about in connection with the fact that in Haya and Ankole, the high tone on the last syllable is realized on the previous syllable.
tone_statements.locator: KAKEN project page KAKENHI-PROJECT-17520258, '2007 Final Research Report Summary' (English), 2nd paragraph (online HTML; no page numbers)
tone_statements.summary: Ankole (Runyankore) has lexical tone (H vs low/toneless words), a system simpler than Haya's; word-final H retracts to the penult; cognate low-toned words surface with antepenultimate H in Nyoro; Tooro to the north has lost lexical tone.

tone_statements.translation: [the acute] marks high tone (H), ˆ marks falling tone (F), and no mark means low tone (L). ... (9) a. H-0 (no H) ... b. H-1 (H on the last syllable; …HL in isolation) ... c. H-2 (H on the second syllable from the end; …HL in isolation) ... As for the comparison of Haya and Ankole: the two languages have basically the same tone system but differ in two points. 1) As seen in secs. 2 and 3, Haya distinguishes all underlying patterns in isolation forms too, whereas Ankole, while retaining the underlying distinctions, does not distinguish the H-1 and H-2 types in isolation except with long vowels. 2) The assignment of words to the patterns differs considerably; in particular, loss of H is conspicuous in Ankole.
tone_statements.locator: p.163; pp.170-171 ex.(9); pp.174-175. '..' = my elisions; '…HL' is the source's own ellipsis.
tone_statements.summary: Ankole nouns: H vs L, at most one H per noun, classes H-0.H-5 by H position from the end (n+1 patterns per n-syllable stem); falling only on long penults; H-1/H-2 merge .HL in isolation; possessive adds a boundary H docking on the noun. Own fieldwork.

tone_statements.citation: Johnson, Lawrence. 1976. Devoicing, tone and stress in Runyankore. In Larry M. Hyman (ed.), Studies in Bantu tonology (Southern California Occasional Papers in Linguistics 3), 207-216. Los Angeles: USC.
tone_statements.quote: Haya and High Runyankore have similar surface tonal patterns in that neither high tone (H) nor falling tone (F) can occur on the final syllable of a word, and there is only one H or F tone per word (F occurring only in penultimate position). Runyankore may have a H tone on the prefix attached to monosyllabic stems. ... As has been shown in all the preceding examples of Low Runyankore, there is an absence of both H and F tones, but a presence of stress.
tone_statements.locator: p. 212, first paragraph.. p. 213, after the Taylor block quote
tone_statements.summary: High speakers: H and F (falling, penultimate only) vs L; at most one H or F per word, never final; tonal minimal pairs; 'carry on' H across words. Low speakers (towns): tones leveled to L, word-penultimate stress instead; author likens the loss to Swahili/Nyakyusa. No count given; 3 = labels H/F/L.

tone.summary: Ankole nouns: H vs L, at most one H per noun, classes H-0.H-5 by H position from the end (n+1 patterns per n-syllable stem); falling only on long penults; H-1/H-2 merge .HL in isolation; possessive adds a boundary H docking on the noun. Own fieldwork.

tone.summary: The article describes a tonal rule, High Tone Bumping, in Runyankore (and other Rutara Bantu languages): a word- or clitic-final H tone shifts a preceding H one syllable leftward, with chains of triggers producing sequences of bumped Hs. It offers two synchronic analyses (a left-to-right iterative rule vs. globally accessed H*-marked tone spans) and discusses the rule's possible historical origin

tone.quote: Haya and High Runyankore have similar surface tonal patterns in that neither high tone (H) nor falling tone (F) can occur on the final syllable of a word, and there is only one H or F tone per word (F occurring only in penultimate position). Runyankore may have a H tone on the prefix attached to monosyllabic stems. ... As has been shown in all the preceding examples of Low Runyankore, there is an absence of both H and F tones, but a presence of stress.
tone.locator: p. 212, first paragraph.. p. 213, after the Taylor block quote
tone.summary: High speakers: H and F (falling, penultimate only) vs L; at most one H or F per word, never final; tonal minimal pairs; 'carry on' H across words. Low speakers (towns): tones leveled to L, word-penultimate stress instead; author likens the loss to Swahili/Nyakyusa. No count given; 3 = labels H/F/L.
